title: End-to-end resource analysis for quantum interior point methods and portfolio optimization
abstract_summary: The authors present a complete end-to-end, circuit-level resource analysis of quantum interior point methods (QIPMs) for second-order cone programming, focused on the portfolio optimization use case. They give explicit quantum circuits and count logical qubits, T-count and T-depth (including constant factors), relate costs to instance-specific parameters (notably a Frobenius condition number and tomography precision), and report numerical experiments on small portfolio instances. Their results show extremely large resource demands (e.g., ∼8×10^6 logical qubits and astronomical T-gate costs for n=100), identify major bottlenecks (ill-conditioned linear systems, costly tomography, and QRAM dependence), and conclude substantial algorithmic improvements are needed for practical quantum advantage.
methodology_description: The authors perform an end-to-end resource analysis and classical numerical simulation study of a Quantum Interior Point Method (QIPM) for solving Second-Order Cone Programs (SOCPs) with a focus on the portfolio-optimization (PO) use case. They (1) map the PO problem to an SOCP via standard reductions (introducing auxiliary variables and a self-dual homogeneous embedding), (2) describe IPM iterations that require solving a Newton linear system at each iteration, (3) replace the linear-system solver subroutine with a state-of-the-art quantum linear system solver (QLSS) built on a discrete-adiabatic evolution construction plus eigenstate filtering (QSVT), (4) specify coherent data access (block-encoding via QRAM and controlled state preparation) and pure-state quantum tomography to extract classical estimates of the normalized solution, (5) derive detailed circuit-level resource counts (logical qubits, T-count, T-depth) including constant factors for all subroutines, and (6) perform classical numerical simulations of the full QIPM pipeline on small, realistic PO instances (random portfolios sampled from historical stock returns) to empirically estimate instance-specific parameters (Frobenius condition number κF, tomography precision ξ, tomographic sample counts k) and then instantiate the resource formulas to report concrete resource numbers for representative problem sizes (notably n=100). Simulations emulate the quantum subroutine by solving linear systems classically and adding multinomial sampling noise consistent with the tomography procedure; an adaptive tomographic-precision selection strategy is used in the simulated IPM loop to ensure neighborhood-of-central-path conditions. The study also investigates simple preconditioning (row normalization) and considers feasible vs infeasible IPM variants (different ways to handle feasibility when using inexact linear solvers).
algorithms_used: Quantum Linear System Solver (QLSS) — discrete adiabatic evolution + eigenstate filtering / QSVT
Classical Interior Point Method (CIPM) / Newton system
experimental_setup: Classical numerical simulation of the full QIPM pipeline. The quantum linear-system subroutine is emulated by solving the linear system exactly on a classical computer and then adding multinomial sampling noise to simulate the outcomes of repeated state-preparation and computational-basis measurements (tomography). The authors run many randomized PO instances (randomly sampled portfolios) and sweep portfolio sizes (n up to 120, often m=2n epochs), collecting empirical values of κF and required tomography precision ξ. An adaptive scheme halves ξ until the computed next iterate lies in the IPM neighborhood.
dataset_used: Historical stock return data from the Dow Jones U.S. Total Stock Market Index (DWCF). Returns for m time epochs (days) are used; m is set proportional to the number of assets (m = 2n in the experiments).

pipeline_steps: Formulate PO instance as SOCP with variables x = (w,ϕ,ρ,t,η) and linear constraints A x = b
Create self-dual homogeneous embedding to obtain trivial initial central point
Iterate IPM: at each iteration compute Newton system (linear system) dependent on current interior point
Apply simple preconditioning: normalize rows of Newton matrix G (D^-1 G) prior to solving
Emulate QLSS: classically solve Newton linear system exactly to get u, normalize u to obtain v; approximate the quantum algorithm by preparing many copies of the normalized state and sampling

Tomography emulation: draw k multinomial samples (k determined by formula k = 57.5 L ln(6L/δ) / (ε^2 (1 - ε^2/4))) to estimate amplitude magnitudes; perform controlled-state procedures in simulation to estimate signs (authors assume sign determination succeeds in simulation)
Adaptive tomography precision: start with ξ large and halve until the resulting next iterate lies in the neighborhood N(γ) of the central path (γ=1/10 used)
Update interior point by stepping a computed step length that enforces target duality-gap reduction factor σ
Record per-iteration metrics κF(G), required ξ, sample counts, and continue until duality gap µ ≤ final ϵ (e.g. 1e-7 for resource computation)

iteration_control.neighborhood_check: classical O(N) test using Tx s and µ; used to adapt tomography precision

key_findings: [supported] We present a complete end-to-end logical-level resource analysis (logical qubits, T-count, T-depth) for a quantum interior point method (QIPM) applied to second-order cone programs (SOCPs) with portfolio optimization (PO) as a case study.

[supported] For a representative PO instance of n = 100 assets and target precision ϵ = 10^-7 we estimate ≈8×10^6 logical qubits, ≈7×10^29 total T gates, and ≈2×10^24 T-layers (T-depth) for the full QIPM run (using empirically observed instance parameters).

[supported] The dominant practical bottlenecks identified are (i) the large number of repeated block-encodings/QRAM accesses, (ii) large Frobenius condition numbers κ_F of the Newton linear systems, (iii) large constant prefactors in state-of-the-art QLSS implementations, and (iv) the high cost of pure-state quantum tomography (ξ^-2 dependence).

[supported] We provide explicit circuits and finite-resource counts for the key subroutines (block-encoding via QRAM, the discrete-adiabatic QLSS, eigenstate-filtering/QSVT, and pure-state tomography) including constant factors.

[supported] We derive and improve finite-sample tomography bounds: to leading order the tomography (using the tomography method analyzed here) requires at most about 115·L·ln(L)/ξ^2 state-preparations/measurements to learn an L-dimensional pure state to ℓ_2 precision ξ (authors' improved constant).

[supported] In numerical simulations on small, realistic PO instances (up to n=120) we observe that the Frobenius condition number κ_F (of the Newton matrix) tends to grow with n and that the required tomography precision ξ tends to shrink with n; for n=100 the median observed κ_F ≈ 1.6×10^4 and median tomographic repetitions k ≈ 3.3×10^8.
[supported] We implement a simple, problem-compatible preconditioner that empirically reduced κ_F by more than an order of magnitude on PO instances at low classical cost.

[supported] We implemented 'feasible' and 'infeasible' QIPM variants (including an IF-QIPM-QR that uses a QR-derived nullspace basis); empirically the infeasible variant performed comparably to feasible variants on our examples despite the infeasible variant lacking the same theoretical guarantees.

[supported] On the tested instances κ_F and ξ^{-1} often plateau (do not diverge) as the IPM duality gap µ → 0; this empirical behaviour contrasted with worst-case theoretical bounds that allow κ_F to grow as 1/µ or 1/µ^2.

[supported] Using the empirically observed parameters and their resource model, even with optimistic hardware clock rates (e.g., 4 GHz QRAM) the estimated wall-clock time remains astronomically large (many thousands of years) for the studied n=100 instance.

[speculative] An asymptotic quantum speedup for IPM-like methods could be achievable in favorable regimes (small κ_F, favourable ξ scaling, efficient QRAM), but that advantage critically depends on instance-specific parameters, preconditioning, and improvements to tomography and QLSS constants.

[speculative] Recent advances in tomography (cited works that reduce dependence from O(L ln L / ξ^2) to O(L ln L / ξ)) or alternative QLSS implementations could reduce resource requirements substantially (authors estimate up to a few orders of magnitude improvement), but not enough by themselves to render the studied instances practical without further innovations.

[speculative] Dedicated hardware QRAM or specialized QRAM-like data-loading hardware might reduce practical overheads, but even under optimistic (and conservative) simplifications the end-to-end cost for the benchmark instance remains prohibitive.

[supported] The paper concludes that, for the PO instances simulated and the current best-known subroutines, large constant pre-factors, ill-conditioning, and the reliance on costly tomography make the QIPM approach impractical, and that fundamental improvements are required for practical quantum advantage.
results_summary: This work performs a detailed end-to-end logical-resource and circuit-level study of quantum interior point methods (QIPMs) for second-order cone programs (SOCPs), demonstrated on concrete portfolio-optimization instances. The authors provide explicit circuits and finite-resource accounting (logical qubits, T-count, T-depth) for block-encoding (QRAM-based), a discrete-adiabatic QLSS with QSVT eigenstate filtering, and pure-state tomography. Numerical simulations on small, realistic PO instances (up to n=120) were used to estimate instance-specific parameters (notably the Frobenius condition number κ_F and tomography precision ξ) and to drive concrete resource estimates. For a representative n=100 instance at target precision ϵ=10^-7 the estimated resources are prohibitively large (≈8×10^6 logical qubits, ≈7×10^29 T gates, ≈2×10^24 T-depth). The authors identify tomography cost, repeated block-encodings (QRAM accesses), large κ_F, and large QLSS constants as independent bottlenecks. They report modest, empirical preconditioning gains and note that feasible/infeasible QIPM variants empirically behave similarly on tested instances. The paper concludes that substantial algorithmic and subroutine-level improvements (and possibly specialized QRAM hardware) are needed before practical quantum advantage is plausible for these problems.

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper does not demonstrate a practical quantum advantage. It shows that, for realistic portfolio instances and current-state subroutines (QRAM-based block-encoding, discrete-adiabatic QLSS with QSVT, and tomography), the resource requirements are astronomically large. The authors note that asymptotic theoretical speedups for QIPM over some classical methods are possible in favorable parameter regimes (e.g., small κ_F and improved tomography scaling), but such regimes were not observed to be practically achievable for the tested PO instances and substantial algorithmic and subroutine-level improvements would be required. Therefore any claimed advantage remains speculative/theoretical rather than demonstrated.
limitations: Extremely large resource requirements: logical qubits (~8×10^6), total T-gates (~7×10^29), and T-depth (~2×10^24) for a modest portfolio size (n = 100, ϵ = 10^-7) — authors conclude these are out of reach in near- and far-term hardware.

Strong dependence on instance-specific parameters: runtime and resource counts depend heavily on the Frobenius condition number κF of Newton matrices and on tomography precision ξ (both vary with problem instance and iteration).
Quantum state tomography is a dominant cost: tomography requires O(L ln L / ξ^2) samples and is the largest contributor to the overall runtime, producing a very large multiplicative overhead.

Large constant prefactors in the QLSS: the best known QLSS implementations have very large constants multiplying κF (authors use a conservative constant C ≈ 2305 and note theoretical bounds can be ≳10^4).

Block-encoding data-loading overheads: QRAM-based block-encoding needs O(L^2) qubits (for minimum-depth constructions used) and has substantial T-depth (O(log(L/εG)) with large practical constants); classical precomputation (angles and gate sequences) is expensive (L^2 polylog(1/ε)).
Poor conditioning of linear systems: even after simple preconditioning, observed κF values can be large (≈10^4 for n=100) and empirically grow with n, which inflates QLSS cost.
Reliance on QRAM: the algorithm requires coherent, large-scale QRAM (assumed available); the QRAM cost and feasibility significantly affect practicality.

Theoretical convergence guarantees are fragile: the original infeasible II-QIPM does not have the same theoretical O(√r) iteration guarantee unless feasibility is preserved — feasible variants require access to a null-space basis, which can be expensive to obtain (e.g., QR decomposition).
Limited numerical evidence: simulations only probe small instances (up to n ≈ 120) so cannot conclusively determine asymptotic scaling of κF and ξ, or whether an asymptotic quantum advantage exists.

Dependence on many error-budget choices and unknown constant factors: overall performance is sensitive to allocations of error budget across block-encoding error, state-preparation error, gate-synthesis, eigenstate-filtering, and tomography.

No physical-level (fault-tolerant) analysis: the paper stops at logical-qubit and T-count/T-depth level and does not fully account for error-correction overheads (physical qubit counts, routing, detailed distillation overheads).

Tomography approach limitations: the chosen tomography protocol has O(1/ξ^2) scaling; while alternatives (e.g., the method of Ref. [34]) can improve asymptotic scaling to O(1/ξ), they may add circuit complexity and constant overheads.

Classical preprocessing and per-iteration classical costs: forming Newton systems and computing residuals, as well as angle synthesis for block-encodings, impose substantial classical time (e.g., O(N^2) per iteration and L^2 polylog(1/ε) for compilation), which constrains speedups.

Multiple independent bottlenecks: tomography, block-encoding cost, large κF, large QLSS constant, and many required iterations each contribute substantially; improving only one is unlikely to make the full pipeline practical.
Empirical variability and sensitivity: ξ and κF show considerable instance-to-instance variability, especially ξ (tomography precision), making worst-case and average-case forecasts uncertain.

[inferred] Practical deployment and integration constraints in real financial workflows (e.g., data confidentiality, regulatory constraints, integration with existing classical infrastructure) are not addressed and may complicate adoption.

[inferred] Even with specialized QRAM hardware and optimistic clock rates, end-to-end runtimes remain prohibitive (authors estimate thousands of years even with a 4 GHz QRAM assumption), implying the approach would still be impractical without algorithmic breakthroughs.

[inferred] The algorithm’s heavy reliance on many large logical qubits and high-depth non-Clifford gates suggests very high requirements for magic-state distillation and error-correction infrastructure, which the logical-level analysis does not quantify.

key_ideas: #idea:near-term-feasibility — End-to-end, circuit-level resource estimates for QIPMs applied to portfolio optimization reveal astronomical costs (e.g., ~8×10^6 logical qubits and extremely large T-gate counts for n=100), implying impracticality in the near term.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Major bottlenecks identified: ill-conditioned Newton linear systems (large Frobenius condition number), very high tomography sample requirements, and explicit QRAM/block-encoding dependence.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Classical components (preconditioning/row-normalization, adaptive tomographic-precision selection, and classical post-processing/emulation) were necessary in the pipeline and partially reduce costs but do not close the gap to practicality.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Authors perform classical emulation of the QLSS (solve linear systems classically and add multinomial sampling noise) and use adaptive tomography to ensure IPM neighborhood conditions — highlighting where quantum subroutines would be inserted and the realistic overheads they introduce.

#limitation:qubit-count — Concrete per-instance empirical fits and formulas show qubit and T-gate resource scaling that make medium-size portfolio instances infeasible under current algorithmic designs.
#limitation:data-encoding — The analysis highlights costly data-access assumptions (coherent block-encoding/QRAM and expensive pure-state tomography) as dominant contributors to resource cost.
contradictions: The paper provides evidence that contradicts optimistic claims of near-term quantum advantage for portfolio optimization: detailed resource accounting shows required resources far exceed plausible near-term or mid-term hardware capabilities.

The reported scaling and instance-based resource estimates contradict claims that quantum interior-point / QLSS-based approaches will scale to practical portfolio sizes without substantial algorithmic change; tomography and QRAM costs in particular break favorable asymptotic arguments.
